foreignObject.h5:div: If the term is unfamiliar to you, here is the short version: System 1 is the
fast, intuitive, and emotional system, while System 2 is the slow,
deliberate, and logical one. Daniel Kahneman, Nobel Prize laureate in
Economics, coined this term in his psychology work on judgment and
decision making, which challenged the idea that humans are rational
TypeSafe leaned into this and named their new type of classification
models “System-One Models”, in contrast to text-generating Large
Language Models (LLMs), which are more like System 2. Jev is their first
How do they compare to LLMs?
LLMs work by predicting the most probable next token, step by step.
Especially for machine-to-machine communication, people have tried to
squeeze LLM output into a schema. There are techniques for that, but they
limit the model in its reasoning capabilities
, and they are nowhere near efficient enough for realtime applications
So what does Jev do differently? It takes the same input as basic LLMs
(which is plain text) and a set of questions with their answer candidates.
Its output is then a set of probabilities for each question. The model
fundamentally does not generate text and therefore cannot return an
mean it cannot pick an incorrect
That reliability and efficiency make it a good fit for realtime
Oh, and they are really really cheap. Jev is currently listed at 0.0047€ per
1M input tokens, with output tokens being free. TypeSafe attributes this
price to the massive parallelism of its decision heads.
Despite Jev having been released only on September 15th, open-weight
alternatives have sprouted up like mushrooms. They mostly work by
architecturally modifying and fine-tuning a pre-trained language model on
a specific dataset. Since the problem space is less fragmented, way
TypeSafe AI claims not to train on your data
, which sounds good on paper. For highly sensitive
applications, like handling health data, this is not enough. Open-
weight models can be self-hosted, which gives the operator more
control over where inference data goes. It does not guarantee that the
whole application keeps no data off-premises.
- 4B params, the open-weight benchmark leader when I started
- ~500MB size, less than 50ms latency even on CPU, often requires
Operating rooms have lots of equipment, and each device brings its own
controls. A voice assistant could save you the constant reaching for knobs
and menus. But a natural command is not enough on its own. The system
has to identify which device and setting the speaker means, handle values
precisely, and avoid changing anything the speaker did not ask to change.

There are a lot of complex components involved to make this work reliably
in the real world. Luckily, the virtual room simplifies things greatly and
allows us to focus on the narrow question of whether a System-One
model can turn short utterances into actionable commands we can
automatically apply to the objects in the room.
The API gives the model the current state, the utterance, and questions
about possible actions to modify the fields/attributes of the objects in the

the application, read more on that

Application code still has to interpret the answer, apply limits, and decide
whether to act based on confidence thresholds. The confidence score of a
is very important, as it cannot name an option outside its
criteria answer space, but it can still choose an incorrect option. So that is
our only way to know how much to trust that confined answer.
In some cases the answer space is trivial, like for the light mode, which is
requested. But what about other continuous fields like the brightness?

locally is important for GDPR compliance. The less hardware is required,
the easier it is to set up for institutions, especially hospitals. So naturally I
wanted to try out how far we can get with one.

In the recorded runs, Jev performs better than JevK5-2B on utterance-level
accuracy. Jev also performs better in the rolling evaluation, where
predictions are applied through an utterance sequence and earlier
mistakes can affect later state. I keep these measurements separate
because JevK5-2B has fewer evaluated cases. The paired comparison in

more than enough to count as real-time interaction. The average human
response time is around 200ms, which is excluding the time to physically
execute the command, so Jev does not lag behind.
“It runs locally” and “it is useful locally” are two different pairs of
on my RTX 2080, but this particular 2B configuration was not fast
enough for the near-real-time interaction I had in mind.
System-One’s constrained outputs are an appealing interface for
equipment-control software. The schema narrows what the model can
return, and the API scores each field directly. That is a much better
JevK5-2B did not turn out to be a practical local substitute for Jev in this
setup. It was less accurate and much slower, and both models missed
nearly every positive safety-interlock case. If privacy is the reason to run
locally, it currently costs more accuracy and latency than I would accept.
So no, local System-One control is not ready. But the failure modes I saw
could be explained by sub-optimal data and instruction setup. Next steps
are to investigate whether better data and more guardrails can close the
gap without moving the safety boundary.
JevK5-2B runs the default checkpoint. I did
not tune it, I just pointed the server at it. My bet is that fine-tuning on
messier utterances, ambiguous phrasing, field boundary cases and
background noise buys more than swapping architectures. That needs
human-reviewed labels instead of the generated ones I used, which
would also make the benchmark mean more than “it works on my
The RTX 2080 is what I had, not what I would buy for this.
A newer card, or a smaller or quantized checkpoint, would probably
bring latency into a comfortable range. Whether that gets below the
~200 ms human response time on hardware a hospital would actually
